commitResults.messageTitle: Update name from Duke to SevenSix
Update the initial code to simply greet the user and exit
Update code to echo user commands and exit with bye
Add ability to store user text and display with list command
Implement mark command to update task status
Implement the unmark command to update task status
Add a test-ui skill to test the code
Update AGENTS.md to use test-ui and review test/ui-test-plan.md
Add typed todo tasks and confirmations
Add deadline tasks with due text
Add event tasks with start and end text
Handle incorrect input and add UI tests
Add support for deleting tasks from the list
Update Task to use TaskType enum instead of hardcoding icon strings
Update UI tests for date handling
Add JUnit tests for parser and storage
Align Gradle and JUnit with duke package
Extract command processing into reusable response methods
Enable assertions when running the chatbot
commitResults.messageBody:
The JVM disables the assert statement unless it is given -ea, so an
assertion in production code documents an assumption without ever
checking it. Gradle's test task enables assertions by default, but the
run task and the recorded console UI tests do not.

Let's,
* set enableAssertions on the run task
* add -ea to each run command in the console UI test plan

Both paths then exercise the same assumptions the JUnit tests already
check, so a broken assumption surfaces during development rather than
reaching a user.

Task, Deadline and Event accept any argument their callers pass. The
description is validated in the command layer and the date fields are
produced by the date parser, so several assumptions hold by
construction but are stated nowhere in these classes.

The nullability rule is the easiest to get wrong: a task always has a
date, while its time is null whenever the user supplies a date on its
own. A reader cannot tell that from the field declarations.

Let's,
* assert that a description is present and a type is set in Task
* assert that Deadline has a date and Event has both endpoints
* assert index and argument assumptions in TaskList

TaskList states the range assumption that SevenSix.getTask already
enforces, which records why get and remove index the list directly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Assert data assumptions for parsing and storage
commitResults.messageBody:
DateTimeParser treats a date as mandatory and a time as optional, and
TaskStorage relies on splitFields returning at least one field before
it counts fields. Neither rule is visible at the point where the code
depends on it.

Let's,
* assert that the date passed to the format methods is present
* assert that parse receives non-blank text
* assert that a storage path is supplied and that splitting a line
  yields at least one field

The format methods are the clearest place to record the rule, because
they are the two methods that would throw an unhelpful
NullPointerException if a date ever went missing.

getResponse decides which handler a command belongs to, and each
handler then cuts its own keyword off the front with substring. The
handlers are private, so that pairing is the only thing that keeps the
cut in range, and nothing in a handler says so.

deleteTask has a second assumption of the same kind: getTask has
already rejected an unusable task number by the time the list is
indexed directly.

Let's,
* assert the expected keyword at the start of each command handler
* assert that the delete index is in range before removing a task
* assert that a task count is never negative and that a data-file
  path is supplied

Stating the assumption in the handler means a future command added to
getResponse with the wrong keyword fails loudly during testing instead
of silently trimming the wrong number of characters.

SevenSix returns raw validation messages from getResponse, while the
console UI plan and tests expect the 676767!!! theme.

This mismatch makes invalid-input responses fail automated tests and
leaves errors inconsistent across commands.

Let's,
* prefix all SevenSixException responses with the 676767!!! marker
* cover unknown-command responses with a JUnit test

Keep the prefix at the shared response boundary so console and GUI
clients receive identical errors.

SevenSix.getResponse handles normalization, command routing, and error
propagation in one long conditional method.

The method is difficult to scan and repeats the same exact-or-prefixed
keyword check for every command, which makes future command additions
more error-prone.

Let's,
* move command routing into a dedicated processCommand method
* centralize exact-or-prefixed keyword matching in isCommand

Keep getResponse focused on normalizing input and translating command
exceptions into responses, while preserving command order and output.

Several collection operations use explicit loops, making common filtering,
mapping, and formatting logic more verbose.

Using Java streams makes these operations more declarative and satisfies the
project's streams requirement while preserving task order and user-visible
output.

Let's,
* refactor task searching and storage conversion to use streams
* generate numbered task output with stream pipelines
Use Assertions
Improve Code Quality

SevenSix cannot reverse a task-changing command after it runs.

Users need a simple way to recover from an accidental recent task change
without manually recreating the previous task list.

Let's,
* add an undo command for the most recent task-changing command
* restore the previous task state and persist it to disk
* add JUnit, CLI, and user-guide coverage for the feature
Add an undo command

SevenSix mixes command parsing, task mutation, persistence, response
formatting, and console I/O within the same methods.

This makes readers switch between user-facing workflows and low-level
implementation details.

Let's,
* extract console setup and command response handling
* separate task parsing, mutation, and response formatting
* centralize numbered task-list formatting

TaskStorage mixes file operations, task serialization, record validation,
task construction, and status restoration.

Separating these stages makes the persistence workflow easier to follow
and keeps each helper at a consistent abstraction level.

Let's,
* separate reading, formatting, and writing operations
* split task-specific record parsing into focused helpers
* isolate completion-status restoration from task construction

The GUI startup method builds every component, configures event handlers,
constructs the layout, and displays the window in one code fragment.

Extracting each UI section makes the startup flow read as a sequence of
high-level interface-building steps.

Let's,
* extract header, conversation, input bar, and layout creation
* separate stage configuration from greeting display
* isolate command-response display from input handling
Refactor codebase for stronger SLAP

SevenSix cannot compile after the Streams merge because the task-list formatter method is incomplete.

The malformed merge leaves task listing code outside a method and adds an
extra unary operator to the find response.

Let's,
* restore the stream-based formatTaskList helper
* correct the find response concatenation

Keep task numbering and console output unchanged.
Use streams

The commit standard states the 72 character limit but gives no way to
check it, and recent commits in this repository have shipped with body
lines well past the limit.

An explicit check turns the limit into something that can be confirmed
before the commit is made, rather than something noticed afterwards when
history can no longer be rewritten safely.

Let's,
* state that the limit applies to every line, including bullet points
* add an awk command that reports over-length lines in a message file
* recommend committing with git commit -F so the verified wrapping is
  the wrapping that is stored
* note that past commits must not be amended to fix wrapping

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a code quality self-check skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Checkstyle covers tabs, line length, braces, casing, and Javadoc
presence, but the course script also reports boolean naming, class size,
method length, dead code, and binary files, none of which Checkstyle
enforces.

Without a written procedure for the uncovered aspects, they are only
found after the script has already reported them.

Let's,
* add a code-quality-self-check skill listing each uncovered aspect and
  the command that verifies it
* require predicate prefixes on boolean locals and parameters, not only
  on fields, in the Java coding standard
* add class and method size guidance to the Java coding standard

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the agent guide at the quality self-check
commitResults.messageBody:
The agent guide describes the coding and commit standards but does not
say that an automated course script checks aspects beyond Checkstyle, so
the self-check has no entry point.

Recording the known problems alongside it keeps them from being
rediscovered on every change, and marks them as existing debt rather
than something to fix unasked.

Let's,
* add a code quality self-check section referencing the new skill
* record the oversized SevenSix class and the non-predicate boolean name
  in TaskStorage as known debt

commitResults.messageTitle: Task storage: name the escape flag as a predicate
commitResults.messageBody:
The local flag tracking whether the previous character was a backslash
is named escaped, which reads as a description of the text rather than
as a question about the parser's state.

The coding standard asks for a predicate prefix on every boolean, and
the self-check grep that enforces it reports this one name.

Let's,
* rename escaped to isEscaped in TaskStorage.splitFields
* narrow the self-check grep so names that already follow the rule are
  filtered out
* record that an action method returning a success flag, such as save,
  keeps its verb name and is not a violation

commitResults.messageTitle: Split SevenSix into parsing, UI, and undo classes
commitResults.messageBody:
SevenSix is around 600 lines. It decides what each command does, but it
also interprets command text, words every reply, drives the console
loop, and deep-copies the task list for undo. Its findTasks method shows
the cost: it extracts a keyword, searches, and then numbers the results
with an index-based stream that duplicates formatTaskList.

A class doing five jobs has no single level of abstraction to read it
at, and the duplicated formatting is the kind of drift that mixing
levels invites.

Let's,
* move command recognition and parsing into a Parser class
* move every user-visible string and the console loop into a Ui class
* move the undo snapshot and its deep copy into an UndoHistory class
* have findTasks reuse the shared task-list formatter
* add an isExactCommand check so bye, list, and undo keep rejecting
  trailing text, as they did when they were compared with equals
* cover Parser and UndoHistory with JUnit tests

The responses are unchanged, so the recorded console UI tests pass
without edits to the plan. SevenSix drops to 293 lines.
Branch fix code quality

The GUI styles each control with inline style strings scattered across
SevenSixGui. The header is a two-line block with large padding, so it
takes a noticeable share of a small window.

Inline styles are hard to keep consistent and cannot express states
such as focus or hover. As the app usually occupies a small part of the
screen, space spent on the header and padding is space taken away from
the conversation.

Let's,
* move all window styling into css/main.css and refer to it through
  style classes
* shrink the header to one slim row holding the title and subtitle
* tighten the padding around the conversation and input bar
* give the command field a focus highlight and the Send button a hover
  state

A stylesheet keeps colors, fonts and spacing in one place, so later
visual tweaks do not need Java changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show user and bot messages in distinct styles
commitResults.messageBody:
User commands and chatbot replies appear as bubbles of the same shape,
differing only in a pale background tint.

The conversation is between a person and an app, not two people. Short
commands and long multi-line replies serve different purposes, and a
chat-between-friends look makes them hard to tell apart at a glance.

Let's,
* show user commands as compact, right-aligned blue bubbles
* show chatbot replies as plain, left-aligned cards with dark text
* replace the boolean DialogBox constructor with getUserDialog and
  getBotDialog factory methods

Named factory methods read more clearly at the call site than a
true/false argument, and leave room for more message kinds.

Error replies, such as the one for an unknown command, look exactly like
ordinary replies in the GUI.

A user who mistypes a command can easily miss that it failed, and may
believe a task was added when it was not.

Let's,
* add Ui.isErrorResponse to recognize replies built by formatError
* show error replies as red-tinted cards with a thick red left edge
* add UiTest to cover recognition of error and normal replies

Ui decides whether a reply is an error because it already owns the
error wording, so the GUI does not need to know the error prefix.

Every message is capped at a fixed 480px width, and the window cannot
be made narrower than 480px.

In a wide window, long replies wrap early and leave empty space beside
them. The fixed minimum size also stops users from tucking the app into
a small corner of the screen.

Let's,
* size messages relative to the conversation width, so they widen and
  narrow as the window is resized
* let chatbot replies use the full width, while user bubbles stay at
  most 80% of it
* lower the minimum window size

Binding the width to the conversation keeps text wrapping correct at
any window size, without a fixed number to tune.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a small round avatar to chatbot replies
commitResults.messageBody:
Messages carry no profile picture, so nothing but position and color
marks who is speaking.

A marker for the chatbot helps the eye find where each reply starts.
The participants never change, so a large picture would only take space
from the text, and an image file would add a binary to the repository.

Let's,
* show a small round badge with the letters 76 beside chatbot replies
* leave user bubbles without an avatar, as their color and alignment
  already identify them

The badge is drawn with JavaFX shapes and styled in the stylesheet, so
it blends with the background and scales cleanly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use a formal prefix for error messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Error messages start with the prefix "676767!!! ", a joke that tells
the user nothing about what the message is.

An unexplained number looks like a glitch rather than a warning, and
makes the app feel unprofessional to new users.

Let's,
* change the error prefix to "Error: "
* update the JUnit and console UI tests to expect the new prefix
* reword the test comments that describe the errors as themed

The GUI still highlights errors, because it recognizes them through
Ui.isErrorResponse rather than by matching the prefix itself.
Improve GUI

commitResults.messageTitle: Give SevenSix a corporate thought-partner voice
commitResults.messageBody:
SevenSix replies in plain, neutral wording that gives the chatbot no
character of its own.

The A-Personality increment asks for a personality that runs through
everything the chatbot says, so that the chatbot is recognisable from
its replies alone.

Let's,
* rewrite every reply in Ui as a corporate productivity coach, where a
  task is a deliverable, the task list is a pipeline, completing a task
  is shipping it, and deleting one is descoping it
* reword the errors thrown by Parser and SevenSix in the same voice, and
  change the error prefix to "Flagging a blocker" to match
* move the greeting into Ui.getGreeting so that the console and the
  graphical interface introduce the chatbot in the same words instead of
  each holding a copy
* update the JUnit tests and the console UI test plan to the new wording

The command syntax is deliberately untouched. Only what SevenSix says
changes, so every command a user already knows keeps working, and the
format examples inside the error messages stay literal.

Error highlighting keeps working because the graphical interface detects
errors through Ui.isErrorResponse rather than by matching the prefix
text.

commitResults.messageTitle: Restyle the window to match the new voice
commitResults.messageBody:
The window uses a generic blue accent and a neutral subtitle that carry
no personality.

The increment asks for a look that goes with the chosen personality, and
a consultant palette reads as deliberate rather than as a default theme.

Let's,
* move the accent colour from blue to teal for the user messages, the
  send button, and the input focus ring
* give the chatbot avatar a warm amber fill so that it reads as a logo
  mark, using a dark enough shade to keep its white label legible
* set a geometric sans font stack, with the system font kept as the last
  fallback so that nothing breaks when a face is missing
* reword the subtitle, the input prompt, and the send button in the
  chatbot's voice, and read the greeting from Ui

Errors keep their red styling. Matching them to the theme would undo the
highlighting that makes them stand out.

The GUI has a compact header and tightly spaced conversation controls.

A clearer visual hierarchy and more breathing room make the app easier
to read and use.

Let's introduce an indigo header, rounded message cards, system fonts,
and a larger command input with usage hints. Adjust window sizing and
text wrapping, centralize GUI labels in Ui, and update the README.

Keep visual styling in CSS so the appearance can evolve independently
of command handling.
Give a unique personality

commitResults.messageTitle: Validate commands and protect task storage
commitResults.messageBody:
Command parsing permits ambiguous parameters and invalid event ranges.
Storage writes can truncate data or hide load failures.

These failures can create misleading tasks or lose saved information.

Let's validate parameters, dates, task identity, and stored records.
Use atomic replacement and block writes after failed or corrupt loads.
Add shared error messages and focused regression tests.

Separate record conversion from filesystem access so each layer can
be checked independently.

commitResults.messageTitle: Roll back failed commands and surface errors
commitResults.messageBody:
Failed saves leave modified tasks in memory and only report errors to
the terminal.

A failed change must preserve tasks and the previous undo opportunity,
and its error must be visible in both interfaces.

Let's restore task state and undo history when a command fails.
Connect validation and startup warnings to both interfaces, and add
integration tests, console regression cases, and recovery instructions.

Keep command handling separate from parsing, wording, and persistence
so error handling follows the existing class responsibilities.

Merge branch-A-MoreErrorHandling

Malformed commands and storage failures can produce invalid tasks or
misleading success responses.

Consistent validation and recoverable failures are needed to protect
task data during normal use.

Let's merge the command-validation and storage-recovery changes.

Preserve tasks and undo history after failed commands, and show clear
errors in both interfaces.

commitResults.messageTitle: Expand JUnit coverage across non-GUI code
commitResults.messageBody:
The test suite leaves gaps in command workflows, persistence, console
interaction, and locale-dependent behaviour.

These gaps allow regressions in core behaviour to go undetected.

Let's expand the suite with parameterized and integration tests, add
JaCoCo reports and coverage checks, and provide a Chinese-locale test
task.

Keep the tests and build configuration together because the new cases
need the parameterized-test dependency and satisfy the coverage gates.
Exclude JavaFX presentation classes while retaining console coverage.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document automated and manual testing workflows
commitResults.messageBody:
The testing instructions lack coverage-report guidance and a GUI test
matrix for different displays, operating systems, and language settings.

Repeatable instructions help contributors verify changes and distinguish
completed checks from checks that still need manual testing.

Let's document test commands, coverage limits and results, and a manual
GUI test plan, with links from the README.

Separate JVM-locale checks from actual OS-language and input-method
tests so that the recorded results do not overstate platform coverage.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix console subprocess test output encoding
commitResults.messageBody:
The subprocess tests decode output as UTF-8 but leave the child
JVM's stdout and stderr encodings dependent on the environment.

This mismatch can corrupt Chinese output and fail assertions even
when task storage preserves the text correctly.

Let's explicitly set both output encodings to UTF-8, verify saved
Unicode content, and include captured output in assertion failures.

This aligns the test's encoding assumptions without changing
production behaviour or weakening the Unicode checks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Avoid Windows launcher encoding in Unicode tests
commitResults.messageBody:
The Windows Java launcher can replace Unicode characters in system
property arguments before the application receives them.

This prevents the subprocess test from reaching its intended task
file, even when console output uses UTF-8.

Let's test subprocess persistence from a Unicode working directory,
verify Unicode configuration separately inside Java, and document
the launcher limitation.

Retain Unicode storage and restart coverage without depending on
the Windows command-line code page. Include captured startup output
to make future failures easier to diagnose.

Merge branch-A-MoreTesting

Automated coverage leaves gaps in core behaviour, and GUI checks
lack a documented cross-platform test plan.

Broader testing is needed to catch regressions reliably.

Let's merge expanded JUnit tests, coverage checks, Chinese-locale
testing, and automated and manual testing documentation.

Keep core behaviour automatically verified while documenting manual
checks for GUI behaviour and platform differences.

Parser and SevenSix contain error wording that belongs in Ui.
Parser also exposes an exact-match helper used only by tests.

Let's,
* centralize command error messages in Ui without changing their text
* remove the unused exact-match helper and its dedicated test
* check all relocated error messages through command-response tests
* correct the task-count return documentation

Keep parsing focused on command structure and Ui responsible for
wording.

The header builder mixes a high-level brand-row helper with inline
label construction and styling, making its abstraction level uneven.

Let's,
* extract introduction label construction into createHeaderCopy
* extract header assembly and styling into createHeaderLayout

Make createHeader read as composition of named steps while preserving
the existing controls, styling, and layout.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract storage test setup and assertions
commitResults.messageBody:
The mixed-task persistence test combines fixture construction with
checks for three task types in a method longer than 30 lines.

Let's,
* extract the mixed-task fixture into a named helper
* group restored-task assertions by task type
* check restored descriptions, to-do type, and event completion status

Keep the save-and-load workflow readable while preserving the existing
checks for ordering, escaping, dates, times, and completion status.

AGENTS.md describes TaskStorage as exceeding 300 lines, but record
encoding now belongs to TaskCodec and TaskStorage is below that size.

Let's remove the resolved class-size debt note so future reviews use
the current implementation rather than an obsolete warning.

Improve command, UI, and test code quality

Command error wording is spread across Parser and SevenSix, while
GUI header construction and storage tests mix multiple levels of detail.
An unused parser helper and outdated documentation add maintenance noise.

Let's,
* centralize command error wording in Ui and verify existing responses
* remove the unused exact-match parser helper and its test
* separate GUI header content construction from layout
* extract storage test setup and task-specific assertions
* correct task-count documentation and remove obsolete storage guidance

Keep command behavior and displayed wording unchanged while making
responsibilities clearer and methods easier to read.

Validation:
* 168 JUnit tests passed
* All 16 recorded console UI tests passed
* Checkstyle and coverage gates passed
* GUI compilation passed; visual testing was not performed

Users cannot inspect command syntax or examples from within SevenSix.
Unknown commands provide only a partial list of available actions.

Let's,
* add help with command syntax, date guidance, and examples
* reject extra help arguments through Parser
* reject Unicode line breaks before whitespace normalization
* test trailing spaces, tabs, Unicode spaces, and end-of-input
* point unknown-command errors and the GUI hint to help
* verify help preserves tasks, saved data, and undo history
* record exact console output for help and updated errors

Keep help wording in Ui so both interfaces share the same guide.

Introduce command help in SevenSix

Users need a way to discover supported commands without leaving the app.

Let's,
* provide help with syntax, date formats, and examples
* keep help read-only and reject extra arguments
* reject Unicode line breaks before whitespace normalization
* test trailing spaces, tabs, Unicode spaces, and end-of-input
* direct users to help from errors and the GUI hint
* cover help with automated tests and usage documentation
* add a manual GUI check for the help response

Share the guide between the console and GUI through Ui.

Validation: JUnit, Checkstyle, coverage gates, and all 19 recorded
console UI cases pass. GUI rendering checks remain manual.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace placeholder documentation with a user guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The template README does not explain how to use SevenSix.

Users need practical examples and guidance on command behaviour
to manage their tasks confidently.

Let's,
* document setup and all supported commands with examples
* explain whitespace, dates, task numbers, and undo limitations
* cover task replacement, saving, backups, and troubleshooting
* include the interface screenshot and clarify v0.2 availability

Use short sections and readable examples to keep the guide easy
to follow.

The project needs user-facing documentation for SevenSix.

Let's bring together the complete user guide and interface
screenshot so users can learn the commands and recover from
common errors.

Clarify that v0.2 is upcoming and provide build instructions
until its JAR is released.
